claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced plastic strain relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has enhanced toughness relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Ti and Zr segregate at grain boundaries in WTaTiVZr.
Ti and Zr grain-boundary segregation promotes the formation of fine, ductile secondary phases.
The secondary phases stabilize the microstructure during thermal-mechanical cycling.
The secondary phases facilitate dislocation mobility.
The secondary phases impede crack propagation.
Ti and Zr segregation reduces local grain-boundary energy.
Ti and Zr segregation forms ductile intermetallic phases at grain boundaries.
The proposed grain-boundary phases blunt crack tips.
Crack-tip blunting and enhanced dislocation mobility delay crack initiation and propagation under high-temperature stress.
Delayed crack initiation and propagation increase plastic strain and toughness.
Under identical high-temperature thermal-mechanical cycling, WTaTiVZr will exhibit statistically significantly greater ductility than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature thermal-mechanical cycling, WTaTiVZr will exhibit statistically significantly greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten.
TEM will reveal pronounced grain-boundary segregation and fine secondary phases in WTaTiVZr that are absent from pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply at approximately 1000–1200°C.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply if WTaTiVZr undergoes phase decomposition or other microstructural instabilities outside the stated temperature window.

Comparing WTaTiVZr only with pure tungsten under matched grain size, atmosphere, temperature, and loading ensures that behavioral differences are attributable solely to alloying-induced microstructural features.
